title: Volumetric vs Mass vs Molar Flow: Which Rate Does Your Process Actually Care About?
h1: Volumetric, mass and molar flow — which one to use
description: Volumetric flow (m³/h) is what pumps deliver. Mass flow (kg/h) is what heat balances need. Molar flow (kmol/h) is what reactions consume. Pick wrong, get wrong.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Compressible gases: volumetric flow varies with T and P. Reactions: molar flow is invariant. Heat exchangers: mass flow drives capacity.
body: Three flow measurements coexist because each answers a different physical question. Pumps and compressors deliver volume, boilers and reactors care about mass or moles.

> Mass flow ṁ = ρ × Q_volumetric
> Molar flow ṅ = ṁ / M (M = molar mass in kg/kmol)
> For an ideal gas: Q at (T₂, P₂) = Q at (T₁, P₁) × (P₁/P₂)(T₂/T₁)

Volumetric (m³/h, gpm, L/min): pump and blower sizing, pipe velocity, dispenser output. Mass (kg/h, lb/hr): heat and mass balances, steam generation, fuel consumption. Molar (kmol/h, lbmol/h): stoichiometric reactions, gas mixing ratios, absorption/stripping columns.

A boiler produces 10 000 kg/h of steam. Volumetric feedwater flow at 80 °C is 10 000 / 972 kg/m³ = 10.29 m³/h. The pump datasheet is in m³/h; the boiler heat rate needs kg/h. Convert once at the boiler nozzle, keep both consistent.
Pumps → m³/h. Boilers → kg/h. Reactors → kmol/h.

faqs.q: Is standard flow mass or volumetric?
faqs.a: It's volumetric — but referenced to a standard T and P (like SCFM). It behaves numerically like a mass flow because the reference density is fixed.

faqs.q: How do I convert m³/h to lb/hr for water?
faqs.a: Multiply m³/h by density (≈999 kg/m³ at 20 °C) then by 2.2046 lb/kg.
